weeks.assessment_key: Final exam sample answers: 1) Scale factor 6→15: 2.5. 2) y = 4x through (3,12). 3) C for d = 10: 31.4. 4) $80 with 15% off: $68. 5) −7 − (−3) = −4. 6) 3x − 5 = 16 → 7. 7) Complement of 38: 52. 8) Prism 3 × 4 × 5: 60. 9) P(sum 7) = 1/6. Investigation rubric: 4 = statistical question, random sample, correct mean/MAD, valid conclusion; 3 = minor errors; 2 = missing parts; 1 = incomplete.

SCI.overview: Science 7 is an integrated, phenomenon-driven course: each unit opens with something puzzling to observe, then builds models and evidence to explain it. Do the hands-on labs together with goggles and an adult at every heat, flame or chemical step; have your child record predictions, data tables and sketches in the notebook every day. Push for claim–evidence–reasoning (CER) explanations that use particle, energy or system models, and use the Friday checks to re-teach before moving on.

weeks.prep: Notebook, goggles, home lab safety contract (write one: goggles on, no tasting, adult for heat/chemicals, wash hands, clean up). Food coloring, hot and cold water, clear cups, balloon, vanilla extract. Bookmark PhET 'Build an Atom'.
misconceptions: Thinking particles stop moving in cold water. All particles are always moving; they move more slowly when colder.
Thinking the balloon must have a hole for the smell to escape. Vanilla molecules are small enough to pass through the gaps between the rubber's molecules.

days.guide: Review each safety rule and why it matters, then sign the contract together. Your child sets up a table of contents and numbers the notebook pages. Check before moving on: ask "What do you do if a chemical splashes into your eye?" Look for: Tell an adult immediately and rinse the eye with running water for at least 15 minutes.

questions.q: What do you do if a chemical splashes into your eye?
questions.a: Tell an adult immediately and rinse the eye with running water for at least 15 minutes.

days.guide: Have your child predict which cup will spread color faster, then drop one drop in each at the same time and time the spreading. They sketch particle models of each cup (dots with motion lines). Check before moving on: ask "Why does the color spread faster in hot water?" Look for: Water particles move faster at higher temperature, so they bump and spread the coloring particles faster.

questions.q: Why does the color spread faster in hot water?
questions.a: Water particles move faster at higher temperature, so they bump and spread the coloring particles faster.

questions.q: Why does it spread at all without stirring?
questions.a: Water particles are constantly moving and colliding with the dye particles (diffusion).

days.guide: Put a few drops of vanilla in a balloon, inflate and tie it, and wait 10 minutes. Your child smells the outside and explains with a particle drawing. Check before moving on: ask "How can you smell vanilla through a sealed balloon?" Look for: Vanilla molecules are tiny and moving; they pass through microscopic gaps between the rubber molecules and reach your nose.

questions.q: How can you smell vanilla through a sealed balloon?
questions.a: Vanilla molecules are tiny and moving; they pass through microscopic gaps between the rubber molecules and reach your nose.

days.guide: Model building hydrogen in PhET (1 proton, 1 electron). Your child builds carbon and oxygen and records protons, neutrons and electrons in a table. Check before moving on: ask "How many protons does carbon have? Oxygen?" Look for: Carbon 6; oxygen 8 (the atomic number).

questions.q: How many protons does carbon have? Oxygen?
questions.a: Carbon 6; oxygen 8 (the atomic number).

questions.q: What determines which element an atom is?
questions.a: The number of protons.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on 'Is matter continuous or made of particles?' using the food coloring and balloon evidence, then takes the vocabulary quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Give one piece of evidence that matter is made of particles." Look for: Vanilla scent passed through the balloon wall, which only makes sense if both are made of particles with spaces between them.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence that matter is made of particles.
questions.a: Vanilla scent passed through the balloon wall, which only makes sense if both are made of particles with spaces between them.

weeks.assessment_key: Vocabulary quiz: matter (anything with mass and volume), particle, atom (smallest unit of an element), element, proton (+), neutron (no charge), electron (−), diffusion. CER rubric: 4 = accurate claim, at least two pieces of specific evidence from the investigation (numbers/observations), reasoning that links evidence to the scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect. Sketches: show particles in both cups, faster motion in hot water.

weeks.prep: Periodic table printout, colored pencils; salt, sand, paper clip bits (or iron filings), magnet, coffee filter, funnel, pan for evaporating (adult for stovetop or leave in the sun).
misconceptions: Thinking salt disappears when it dissolves. It is still there — evaporate the water to get it back.
Calling any pure-looking substance an element. Water and salt are compounds (two or more elements chemically bonded).

days.guide: Your child hunts for 10 elements at home (aluminum foil — Al, copper wire — Cu, pencil 'lead' — C as graphite, iron nail — Fe, helium balloon — He, etc.) and finds each on the table. Check before moving on: ask "Symbol for aluminum? For iron?" Look for: Al; Fe.

questions.a: Al; Fe.
No — it is graphite, a form of carbon, mixed with clay.

days.guide: Model reading the box for carbon (atomic number 6, symbol C, mass ≈ 12.01). Your child records 15 elements and colors metals, nonmetals and metalloids along the staircase line. Check before moving on: ask "What does atomic number tell you?" Look for: The number of protons in each atom of that element.

questions.q: What does atomic number tell you?
questions.a: The number of protons in each atom of that element.

questions.q: Is silicon a metal, nonmetal or metalloid?
questions.a: Metalloid.

days.guide: Your child plans the separation order, then does it: magnet pulls out the clips, add water to dissolve salt, filter out sand, evaporate the water to recover salt. Check before moving on: ask "Why must you filter before evaporating?" Look for: Filtering removes the sand; evaporating then leaves only the salt that was dissolved.

questions.q: Why must you filter before evaporating?
questions.a: Filtering removes the sand; evaporating then leaves only the salt that was dissolved.

questions.q: Which property does each step use?
questions.a: Magnetism (iron), solubility (salt dissolves, sand doesn't), particle size (filter), boiling point (water evaporates).

days.guide: Define element, compound and mixture. Your child sorts 12 substances with one-sentence justifications. Check before moving on: ask "Classify water, air, salt, trail mix, sugar, gold." Look for: Water — compound; air — mixture; salt — compound; trail mix — mixture; sugar — compound; gold — element.

questions.q: Classify water, air, salt, trail mix, sugar, gold.
questions.a: Water — compound; air — mixture; salt — compound; trail mix — mixture; sugar — compound; gold — element.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "How is a compound different from a mixture?" Look for: A compound has elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and can't be separated physically; a mixture's parts keep their own properties and can be separated physically.

questions.q: How is a compound different from a mixture?
questions.a: A compound has elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and can't be separated physically; a mixture's parts keep their own properties and can be separated physically.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Element = one kind of atom. 2) Compound = two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (H2O). 3) Mixture = physically combined, separable (sand + salt). 4) Na = sodium, atomic number 11. 5) O has 8 protons. 6) Metals are on the left/center, nonmetals upper right. Lab write-up: correct order (magnet → dissolve → filter → evaporate) with the property used at each step.

weeks.prep: Gumdrops or mini marshmallows in 4 colors, toothpicks; salt and sugar crystals, magnifier; PhET 'Build a Molecule'.
misconceptions: Reading the subscript as applying to the element before AND after it. In CO2 the 2 belongs only to O.
Thinking salt is made of separate 'NaCl molecules'. It is an extended repeating lattice of Na and Cl ions.

days.guide: Model counting atoms in H2O. Your child counts atoms in CO2, O2, CH4 and C6H12O6. Check before moving on: ask "Atoms in C6H12O6?" Look for: 6 C, 12 H, 6 O = 24 atoms.

questions.a: 6 C, 12 H, 6 O = 24 atoms.
1 carbon and 4 hydrogen = 5.

days.guide: Set a color key (e.g., black = C, white = H, red = O, blue = N). Your child builds H2O, CO2, CH4 and NH3. Check before moving on: ask "Draw ammonia." Look for: One nitrogen bonded to three hydrogens (NH3).

questions.a: One nitrogen bonded to three hydrogens (NH3).

questions.q: How many toothpicks connect atoms in CH4?
questions.a: 4 — each H bonds to the central C.

days.guide: Your child assembles 8 molecules in PhET and records formula and name. Check before moving on: ask "What does the formula O2 show?" Look for: A molecule of two oxygen atoms bonded together (the oxygen we breathe).

questions.q: What does the formula O2 show?
questions.a: A molecule of two oxygen atoms bonded together (the oxygen we breathe).

days.guide: Look at salt crystals (cubes) and sugar crystals under a magnifier. Your child builds a 3×3×3 alternating NaCl lattice. Check before moving on: ask "Why are salt crystals cube-shaped?" Look for: Sodium and chloride ions repeat in a cubic pattern, so the crystal grows as cubes.

questions.a: Sodium and chloride ions repeat in a cubic pattern, so the crystal grows as cubes.

days.guide: Your child draws and labels three molecules and one extended structure and explains the difference. Check before moving on: ask "Molecule vs. extended structure?" Look for: A molecule is a small group of a fixed number of atoms; an extended structure is a repeating pattern that continues in all directions (salt, diamond, metals).

questions.a: A molecule is a small group of a fixed number of atoms; an extended structure is a repeating pattern that continues in all directions (salt, diamond, metals).

weeks.assessment_key: Check drawings: H2O (bent, O center with 2 H), CO2 (O=C=O, linear), CH4 (C with 4 H), plus NaCl lattice with alternating ions. Explanation proficient: molecules have a set number of atoms; extended structures repeat with no set size.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (grams), measuring cup with mL, water, vegetable oil, corn syrup, grape, cork, coin; salt, sugar, baking soda, teaspoon; vinegar, iodine (tincture, adult handles); cornstarch, baking soda and sugar as 'mystery powders' in labeled cups A–C.
misconceptions: Thinking heavy objects always sink. Sinking depends on density compared with the liquid.
Forgetting to subtract the container's mass. Tare the scale or subtract.

days.guide: Model density = mass ÷ volume with 100 mL of water (≈100 g → 1.0 g/mL). Your child measures oil and corn syrup and calculates. Check before moving on: ask "50 mL of oil has a mass of 46 g. Density?" Look for: 0.92 g/mL — less than water, so oil floats on water.

questions.q: 50 mL of oil has a mass of 46 g. Density?
questions.a: 0.92 g/mL — less than water, so oil floats on water.
Corn syrup (~1.3–1.4 g/mL) > water (1.0) > oil (~0.92).

days.guide: Your child pours corn syrup, then water, then oil slowly down the side and predicts where each object settles before dropping it. Check before moving on: ask "Where do the coin, grape and cork settle?" Look for: Coin on the bottom; grape usually sinks through water and rests on the corn syrup; cork floats on the oil.

questions.q: Where do the coin, grape and cork settle?
questions.a: Coin on the bottom; grape usually sinks through water and rests on the corn syrup; cork floats on the oil.

days.guide: Your child adds one level teaspoon at a time to 100 mL room-temperature water, stirring until no more dissolves, and graphs teaspoons dissolved. Check before moving on: ask "Which dissolves the most?" Look for: Sugar dissolves by far the most, salt a moderate amount (~36 g per 100 mL), baking soda the least (~10 g).

questions.a: Sugar dissolves by far the most, salt a moderate amount (~36 g per 100 mL), baking soda the least (~10 g).

days.guide: Your child tests each powder (dissolves? feel? vinegar? iodine?) and uses a key. Check before moving on: ask "Which powder turns blue-black with iodine?" Look for: Cornstarch — iodine detects starch.

questions.q: Which powder turns blue-black with iodine?
questions.a: Cornstarch — iodine detects starch.
Baking soda — it reacts to produce carbon dioxide gas.

days.guide: Your child writes a lab report: question, hypothesis, materials, procedure, data table, conclusion. Check before moving on: ask "Why test with several properties?" Look for: One property alone may match more than one substance; several properties identify it with confidence.

questions.a: One property alone may match more than one substance; several properties identify it with confidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Density calculations correct to 2 decimal places with units g/mL. Lab report rubric: 4 = complete data table for all tests, correct IDs (fizz = baking soda, blue-black with iodine = cornstarch, dissolves with no reaction = sugar), conclusion cites data; 3 = one ID weakly supported; 2 = missing data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Milk, white vinegar, strainer, paper towels; white school glue (PVA), borax, water (adult mixes borax solution; wash hands); 15 household items.
misconceptions: Thinking 'synthetic' means not from nature at all. Synthetics are made from natural resources (often petroleum) changed by chemical processes.
Thinking slime is a new element. It's a polymer: long chains linked by borate.

days.guide: Your child sorts 15 items (cotton shirt, wool, nylon backpack, plastic bottle, wood, rubber band…) and traces three synthetics to raw resources. Check before moving on: ask "What raw resource are most plastics made from?" Look for: Petroleum (crude oil) and natural gas.

questions.q: What raw resource are most plastics made from?
questions.a: Petroleum (crude oil) and natural gas.

questions.q: Nylon or cotton — which is synthetic?
questions.a: Nylon.

days.guide: Warm 1 cup milk (not boiling), stir in 4 tsp vinegar, strain the curds, press dry, mold and let dry 48 hours. Your child records observations. Check before moving on: ask "What new substance formed?" Look for: Casein, a protein polymer that clumps when acid is added — an early plastic.

questions.a: Casein, a protein polymer that clumps when acid is added — an early plastic.

days.guide: Mix glue and water, then add borax solution while stirring. Your child compares slime with glue and borax solution. Check before moving on: ask "Why is slime stretchy?" Look for: Borate links PVA polymer chains loosely into a network.

questions.a: Borate links PVA polymer chains loosely into a network.

days.guide: Your child researches one material and writes about how it's made and its impacts. Check before moving on: ask "Environmental issue with plastic bags?" Look for: They last hundreds of years, break into microplastics and harm wildlife.

questions.a: They last hundreds of years, break into microplastics and harm wildlife.

days.guide: Give unit 1 test; infographic presentation. Check before moving on: ask "Example of a synthetic material from a natural resource?" Look for: Nylon from petroleum.

questions.q: Example of a synthetic material from a natural resource?
questions.a: Nylon from petroleum.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test: particles move faster when hot; element/compound/mixture classification; count atoms in formulas; density calculations; synthetic materials come from natural resources via chemical reactions. Infographic: raw resource, process, uses, impact.

weeks.prep: Nails (new and rusty), steel wool (soap-free), jar; baking soda, vinegar, milk, lemon juice, Alka-Seltzer, ice, sugar, candle and matches (adult), bread and toaster.
misconceptions: Thinking any change in appearance is chemical. Melting ice and dissolving sugar are physical: no new substance.
Thinking bubbles always mean a chemical reaction. Boiling water bubbles but is physical.

days.guide: Compare nails: color, texture, magnetism, strength. Start the steel-wool jar (wet steel wool with vinegar, rinse, place in jar). Check before moving on: ask "What is rust?" Look for: Iron oxide — a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

questions.a: Iron oxide — a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

days.guide: Your child runs four mini-reactions and records evidence (gas, color change, precipitate/solid, temperature change). Check before moving on: ask "Evidence in milk + lemon juice?" Look for: Curdling — a new solid forms.

questions.a: Curdling — a new solid forms.
Bubbles of gas (CO2) and a temperature drop.

days.guide: Test each change; your child classifies with evidence. Check before moving on: ask "Burning candle?" Look for: Chemical — new substances (CO2, water vapor, soot), light and heat.

questions.a: Chemical — new substances (CO2, water vapor, soot), light and heat.
Physical — still water.

days.guide: Your child analyzes a before/after property table. Check before moving on: ask "A substance with different melting point, density and color after mixing — new substance?" Look for: Yes, changed characteristic properties mean a new substance formed.

questions.q: A substance with different melting point, density and color after mixing — new substance?
questions.a: Yes, changed characteristic properties mean a new substance formed.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on rusting using the jar observations. Check before moving on: ask "Is rusting chemical?" Look for: Yes — new substance with different color, texture, and it's not magnetic like iron.

questions.a: Yes — new substance with different color, texture, and it's not magnetic like iron.

weeks.assessment_key: Reaction evidence chart: four reactions with gas/color/solid/temperature evidence. CER rubric: 4 = accurate claim, at least two pieces of specific evidence from the investigation (numbers/observations), reasoning that links evidence to the scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect. Expected claim: rusting is a chemical reaction because a reddish-brown, crumbly substance with different properties forms.

weeks.prep: LEGO bricks in 3 colors (or gumdrops); PhET 'Balancing Chemical Equations'.
misconceptions: Changing subscripts to balance. Subscripts change the substance; only change coefficients.
Thinking atoms are destroyed in a reaction. Atoms rearrange; the same atoms appear on both sides.

days.guide: Model labeling reactants, products, coefficients and subscripts in 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Your child labels five equations. Check before moving on: ask "In 2H2O, how many hydrogen atoms?" Look for: 4 (2 molecules × 2 H).

questions.a: 4 (2 molecules × 2 H).

questions.q: What are the reactants in CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O?
questions.a: Methane and oxygen.

days.guide: Build methane and 2 oxygen molecules from LEGO, take them apart, rebuild into CO2 and 2 H2O. Your child counts atoms before and after. Check before moving on: ask "Atom counts both sides?" Look for: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O on each side.

questions.a: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O on each side.

days.guide: Your child completes PhET intro and game levels 1–2. Check before moving on: ask "Balance H2 + O2 → H2O." Look for: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

Model NaHCO3 + CH3COOH → NaCH3COO + H2O + CO2. Your child explains where the gas comes from. Check before moving on: ask "Where does the gas come from?" Look for: Carbon and oxygen atoms from the baking soda rearrange into carbon dioxide gas.

questions.q: Where does the gas come from?
questions.a: Carbon and oxygen atoms from the baking soda rearrange into carbon dioxide gas.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Balance N2 + H2 → NH3." Look for: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) 3CO2 has 3 C, 6 O. 2) Balance Mg + O2 → MgO: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. 3) Balance H2 + Cl2 → HCl: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. 4) Balance N2 + H2 → NH3: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. 5) Coefficient vs subscript explained.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (0.1 g ideal), plastic bottle, balloon, baking soda, vinegar, Alka-Seltzer, graph paper. Short reading on Lavoisier.
misconceptions: Thinking mass is lost when gas escapes. It goes into the air; in a closed system the mass stays the same.
Thinking gases have no mass.

days.guide: Mass cup + vinegar + baking soda (separately on the scale) before, react in open cup, mass after. Your child calculates apparent loss. Check before moving on: ask "Why did mass decrease?" Look for: CO2 gas escaped into the air.

questions.a: CO2 gas escaped into the air.

days.guide: Put baking soda in balloon, vinegar in bottle, mass everything, tip baking soda in, mass again. Check before moving on: ask "What happened to the mass?" Look for: It stayed the same (within measurement error) because the gas was trapped.

questions.a: It stayed the same (within measurement error) because the gas was trapped.

days.guide: Your child draws particle models for open and closed systems. Check before moving on: ask "What's the difference?" Look for: In open system, gas particles leave; in closed system, all atoms stay.

questions.a: In open system, gas particles leave; in closed system, all atoms stay.

days.guide: Read about Lavoisier; your child summarizes. Check before moving on: ask "What did Lavoisier show?" Look for: In closed containers, mass is conserved during reactions — mass of reactants equals mass of products.

questions.a: In closed containers, mass is conserved during reactions — mass of reactants equals mass of products.

days.guide: Your child writes the lab report. Check before moving on: ask "State the law of conservation of mass." Look for: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

questions.q: State the law of conservation of mass.
questions.a: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: question, hypothesis, data table (open and closed masses), graph, conclusion explaining gas escape vs trapped gas using conservation of mass.

weeks.prep: Thermometer (digital ideal), baking soda, vinegar, 3% hydrogen peroxide, dry yeast, steel wool, jar, calcium chloride (ice melt; gloves).
misconceptions: Thinking a 'cold' reaction adds cold. Endothermic reactions absorb thermal energy from surroundings, so the surroundings get colder.
Thinking all reactions get hot.

days.guide: Your child records temperature every 30 seconds for baking soda + vinegar and graphs. Check before moving on: ask "What happens to the temperature?" Look for: It drops a few degrees — the reaction absorbs energy (endothermic).

questions.a: It drops a few degrees — the reaction absorbs energy (endothermic).

days.guide: Your child tests yeast + peroxide and steel wool + vinegar in a jar. Check before moving on: ask "Temperature change in yeast + peroxide?" Look for: It rises — exothermic (releases energy) as peroxide breaks into water and oxygen.

questions.a: It rises — exothermic (releases energy) as peroxide breaks into water and oxygen.

days.guide: Compare graphs and classify. Check before moving on: ask "Steel wool rusting?" Look for: Exothermic — temperature rises slowly.

questions.a: Exothermic — temperature rises slowly.

days.guide: Read about hand warmers and cold packs. Check before moving on: ask "What makes hand warmers hot?" Look for: Iron powder oxidizing (rusting) quickly with air, helped by salt.

questions.a: Iron powder oxidizing (rusting) quickly with air, helped by salt.
Ammonium nitrate (or urea) dissolving in water absorbs energy.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Define exothermic." Look for: A reaction that releases thermal energy to its surroundings.

questions.a: A reaction that releases thermal energy to its surroundings.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Exothermic releases energy (temp rises). 2) Endothermic absorbs energy (temp falls). 3) Baking soda + vinegar = endothermic. 4) Hand warmer = exothermic iron oxidation. 5) Graph rising = exothermic.

weeks.prep: Zip bags, calcium chloride, baking soda, citric acid, water, thermometer, scale, gloves, goggles.
misconceptions: Changing more than one variable between prototypes.
Ignoring constraints (safety, cost) once something works.

days.guide: Your child writes criteria (e.g., changes 10 °C for 5 minutes) and constraints (safe, under 50 g, cheap). Check before moving on: ask "Criteria vs constraints?" Look for: Criteria = what success looks like; constraints = limits.

questions.a: Criteria = what success looks like; constraints = limits.

days.guide: Build and test two designs with different amounts of reactants. Check before moving on: ask "Which reactants for a warmer?" Look for: Calcium chloride + water (exothermic).

questions.a: Calcium chloride + water (exothermic).
Citric acid + baking soda + water (endothermic).

days.guide: Your child compares tests in a decision matrix and redesigns. Check before moving on: ask "What's a decision matrix?" Look for: A table scoring designs on each criterion to pick the best.

questions.a: A table scoring designs on each criterion to pick the best.

days.guide: Test improved design three times and average. Check before moving on: ask "Why test three times?" Look for: To check reliability and reduce effect of errors.

questions.a: To check reliability and reduce effect of errors.

days.guide: Present design; unit 2 test. Check before moving on: ask "Why does more calcium chloride make it warmer?" Look for: More reacting particles release more total energy.

questions.q: Why does more calcium chloride make it warmer?
questions.a: More reacting particles release more total energy.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio: criteria/constraints, two prototypes with data, decision matrix, improved design average. Unit 2 test: signs of chemical change, balancing, conservation of mass, endo/exothermic.

weeks.prep: Fresh spinach, baking soda, dish soap (1 drop), plastic syringe (no needle), hole punch or straw, clear cups, desk lamp, timer; short reading on van Helmont's willow experiment; gumdrops and toothpicks.
misconceptions: Believing plant mass comes from soil. Van Helmont's soil lost only a few ounces; most mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air (plus water).
Thinking plants don't need oxygen or don't respire. Plants do both photosynthesis and cellular respiration.

days.guide: Read about van Helmont: a 5-lb willow grew to about 169 lb in 5 years while the soil lost only about 2 ounces. Your child predicts where the mass came from and records the prediction. Check before moving on: ask "What did van Helmont conclude, and what was he missing?" Look for: He concluded the mass came from water; he missed that carbon dioxide from the air supplies most of the mass (carbon).

questions.q: What did van Helmont conclude, and what was he missing?
questions.a: He concluded the mass came from water; he missed that carbon dioxide from the air supplies most of the mass (carbon).

days.guide: Punch 10 leaf disks, pull air out with the syringe in baking-soda water until they sink, place under the lamp and count floating disks each minute. Your child records in a table. Check before moving on: ask "Why do the disks float?" Look for: Photosynthesis makes oxygen gas that collects in the leaf, making disks less dense.

questions.a: Photosynthesis makes oxygen gas that collects in the leaf, making disks less dense.
It supplies carbon dioxide (as bicarbonate) for photosynthesis.

days.guide: Repeat at two or three lamp distances. Your child graphs minutes-to-float versus distance. Check before moving on: ask "Prediction for a farther lamp?" Look for: Disks float more slowly because less light means less photosynthesis.

questions.a: Disks float more slowly because less light means less photosynthesis.

days.guide: Build 6CO2 + 6H2O with gumdrops, rearrange into C6H12O6 + 6O2. Your child counts atoms. Check before moving on: ask "Atom count each side?" Look for: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O.

questions.a: Light energy is stored in the sugar's chemical bonds.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER. Check before moving on: ask "Claim?" Look for: Most of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, built into sugar during photosynthesis.

questions.a: Most of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, built into sugar during photosynthesis.

weeks.assessment_key: Leaf-disk data: table and graph showing faster floating with more light. CER rubric: 4 = accurate claim, at least two pieces of specific evidence from the investigation (numbers/observations), reasoning that links evidence to the scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect.

weeks.prep: Dry yeast, sugar, warm water, 3 bottles, 3 balloons, string and ruler; red cabbage indicator (boil chopped red cabbage, cool, strain — adult) or bromothymol blue; straws.
misconceptions: Thinking only animals do respiration.
Confusing breathing with cellular respiration. Breathing moves air; cellular respiration releases energy from food in cells.

days.guide: Set up bottles with 0, 1 and 2 tbsp sugar and yeast in warm water, balloons on top. Your child measures circumference every 10 minutes. Check before moving on: ask "Which balloon inflates most?" Look for: The one with the most sugar — more food for respiration means more CO2.

questions.a: The one with the most sugar — more food for respiration means more CO2.
Carbon dioxide.

days.guide: Your child blows gently through a straw into indicator at rest, then after 1 minute of jumping jacks, and compares. Check before moving on: ask "What color change shows CO2?" Look for: Red cabbage shifts toward pink/red (more acidic); bromothymol blue turns green to yellow.

questions.a: Red cabbage shifts toward pink/red (more acidic); bromothymol blue turns green to yellow.
Muscles do more respiration and release more CO2.

days.guide: Write both equations. Your child diagrams how they cycle. Check before moving on: ask "Respiration equation?" Look for: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy.

questions.a: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy.
Products of one are reactants of the other.

days.guide: Model food broken into smaller molecules that cells rebuild. Check before moving on: ask "What happens to proteins you eat?" Look for: Broken into amino acids then rebuilt into your body's proteins.

questions.q: What happens to proteins you eat?
questions.a: Broken into amino acids then rebuilt into your body's proteins.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Where does cellular respiration occur?" Look for: In the mitochondria of cells.

questions.a: In the mitochondria of cells.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Respiration equation. 2) Plants do photosynthesis AND respiration. 3) CO2 test with indicator. 4) Yeast with more sugar made more CO2. 5) Mitochondria. Yeast data table: circumference readings with units.

weeks.prep: Iodine (adult), brown paper bag, bread, potato, oil, butter, cracker; five nutrition labels; cheese puff, soda can, thermometer, paper clip stand, matches (adult only, outdoors or over sink).
misconceptions: Thinking Calories are an ingredient. A Calorie is a unit of energy.
Thinking all food energy is used immediately.

days.guide: Your child tests foods with iodine (blue-black = starch) and brown paper (translucent spot = fat). Check before moving on: ask "Potato with iodine?" Look for: Turns blue-black — contains starch.

questions.a: Turns blue-black — contains starch.
Leaves a translucent grease spot — fat.

days.guide: Your child compares five labels; note fat = 9 Cal/g, carbs and protein = 4 Cal/g. Check before moving on: ask "A snack with 10 g fat — Calories from fat?" Look for: 90 Calories.

questions.q: A snack with 10 g fat — Calories from fat?
questions.a: 90 Calories.

days.guide: Adult burns a cheese puff under a can with 50 mL water. Your child calculates. Check before moving on: ask "Water 50 g rises 10 °C. Energy?" Look for: 50 × 10 = 500 calories = 0.5 food Calories (about 2,090 J).

questions.a: 50 × 10 = 500 calories = 0.5 food Calories (about 2,090 J).

days.guide: Read and flowchart protein to amino acids to body proteins. Check before moving on: ask "Why can't the body use whole proteins from food?" Look for: They must be broken down into amino acids to be absorbed and rearranged.

questions.q: Why can't the body use whole proteins from food?
questions.a: They must be broken down into amino acids to be absorbed and rearranged.

days.guide: Your child explains how a sandwich becomes energy and muscle. Check before moving on: ask "Key answer?" Look for: Digestion breaks food into small molecules; cells use sugars in respiration for energy and rebuild amino acids into muscle.

questions.a: Digestion breaks food into small molecules; cells use sugars in respiration for energy and rebuild amino acids into muscle.

weeks.assessment_key: Results table: starch in bread/potato, fat in butter/oil. Explanation rubric: digestion, absorption, respiration for energy, synthesis for growth; mentions atoms rearranged.

weeks.prep: A sealed jar with a sprig of an aquatic plant (elodea) or small potted plant (optional snail), or use data from a video of a sealed bottle garden; poster paper, markers; flashcards.
misconceptions: Saying energy cycles like matter. Matter (atoms) cycles; energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat — it flows one way.
Thinking plants photosynthesize but don't respire. Plants respire all the time; in light, photosynthesis is faster than respiration.

days.guide: Show the sealed-jar data (e.g., O2 and CO2 levels by day and night). Your child explains how plant and snail both survive, and what would happen in total darkness. Check before moving on: ask "How do the plant and snail survive in a sealed jar?" Look for: The plant uses light, CO2 and water to make sugar and O2; the snail uses O2 and releases CO2; decomposers recycle waste.

questions.q: How do the plant and snail survive in a sealed jar?
questions.a: The plant uses light, CO2 and water to make sugar and O2; the snail uses O2 and releases CO2; decomposers recycle waste.

questions.q: What if the jar were kept dark?
questions.a: Photosynthesis stops; oxygen runs out and both eventually die.

days.guide: Brainstorm the journey together, then your child writes a first-person story of a carbon atom traveling from the air into a leaf, a rabbit and back to the air, naming each process. Check before moving on: ask "Name the process at each step." Look for: Air → leaf: photosynthesis (into glucose); leaf → rabbit: eating/digestion; rabbit → air: cellular respiration releases CO2.

questions.q: Name the process at each step.
questions.a: Air → leaf: photosynthesis (into glucose); leaf → rabbit: eating/digestion; rabbit → air: cellular respiration releases CO2.

days.guide: Your child draws a poster linking photosynthesis and respiration, with one color for matter arrows (CO2, H2O, O2, sugar) and another for energy (light in, heat out). Check before moving on: ask "Which arrows make a loop and which don't?" Look for: Matter arrows make a loop; energy arrows go in one direction (sunlight → chemical energy → heat).

questions.q: Which arrows make a loop and which don't?
questions.a: Matter arrows make a loop; energy arrows go in one direction (sunlight → chemical energy → heat).

days.guide: Quiz with flashcards, then your child completes a practice set on unit 3; re-teach any missed term. Check before moving on: ask "Reactants and products of photosynthesis?" Look for: Reactants: CO2 and H2O (with light energy); products: glucose (C6H12O6) and O2.

questions.a: Reactants: CO2 and H2O (with light energy); products: glucose (C6H12O6) and O2.

days.guide: Give the unit 3 test independently. Check before moving on: ask "Where does most of a plant's mass come from?" Look for: Carbon dioxide from the air.

questions.q: Where does most of a plant's mass come from?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide from the air.

weeks.assessment_key: Carbon story rubric: correct path and process names at each step (photosynthesis, digestion, respiration) = proficient. Poster: matter loops, energy flows one way, both equations shown. Unit 3 test: 1) photosynthesis equation; 2) respiration equation; 3) mass mostly from CO2; 4) leaf disks float from O2; 5) yeast CO2 increases with sugar; 6) fat 9 Cal/g, carbs/protein 4 Cal/g; 7) food molecules broken down and rebuilt.

weeks.prep: Dried beans (food, water, shelter piles), graph paper; lynx–hare data (Hudson's Bay Company pelt records, widely available online); radish seeds, 3 cups of soil, ruler.
misconceptions: Thinking a population keeps growing if there's food. Other limiting factors (water, space, disease, predators) cap it at carrying capacity.
Thinking predators wipe out their prey. In cycles, predator numbers fall after prey decline, letting prey recover.

days.guide: Explain the 'Oh Deer!' rules: each 'deer' (bean) needs a resource each round; deer that find one reproduce, those that don't die. Play 15 rounds, varying resources, and your child graphs the population. Check before moving on: ask "Describe the graph's pattern." Look for: The population rises when resources are plentiful and falls when they run short, oscillating over time.

questions.a: The population rises when resources are plentiful and falls when they run short, oscillating over time.

days.guide: Your child graphs or reads the lynx–hare data and describes the pattern. Check before moving on: ask "What pattern do you see?" Look for: Both cycle about every 10 years; lynx peaks come shortly after hare peaks.

questions.a: Both cycle about every 10 years; lynx peaks come shortly after hare peaks.

days.guide: Your child plants radishes at 3, 10 and 30 seeds per cup, same soil, water and light, and predicts results (check over the next weeks). Check before moving on: ask "Prediction for the 30-seed cup?" Look for: Smaller, thinner plants because they compete for light, water and nutrients.

questions.a: Smaller, thinner plants because they compete for light, water and nutrients.

days.guide: Show an S-shaped (logistic) growth graph. Your child marks where growth is fastest and where carrying capacity is reached, and lists limiting factors. Check before moving on: ask "What is carrying capacity?" Look for: The largest population an environment can support over time with its resources.

questions.a: The largest population an environment can support over time with its resources.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Name two density-dependent limiting factors." Look for: Competition for food; disease; predation.

questions.a: Competition for food; disease; predation.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Limiting factor = resource or condition that limits population growth (food, water, shelter, space). 2) Carrying capacity definition. 3) S-curve flattens at carrying capacity. 4) Lynx peaks lag hare peaks. 5) Crowded plants are smaller due to competition. Population graph: rounds on x-axis, deer on y-axis, labeled.

weeks.prep: 20 organism-pair cards (e.g., bee/flower, tick/dog, remora/shark, lion/zebra, two trees for light), notebook, timer for outdoor survey.
misconceptions: Mixing up mutualism (both benefit) and commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected).
Thinking competition only happens between different species. Members of the same species compete too.

days.guide: Define the five interaction types with an example each. Your child sorts the 20 cards and justifies each. Check before moving on: ask "Bee and flower?" Look for: Mutualism — the bee gets nectar, the flower gets pollinated.

questions.a: Mutualism — the bee gets nectar, the flower gets pollinated.
Commensalism — barnacles get a ride and food; the whale is mostly unaffected.

days.guide: Spend 30 quiet minutes outside. Your child records organisms, counts and any interactions (a bird eating seeds, ants on a plant). Check before moving on: ask "Why sit still and quiet?" Look for: Animals return and behave naturally when not disturbed.

questions.a: Animals return and behave naturally when not disturbed.

days.guide: Your child compares one example of each interaction in a kelp forest, desert and rainforest. Check before moving on: ask "What pattern repeats across ecosystems?" Look for: All have predation, competition and mutualism, even though the organisms differ.

questions.a: All have predation, competition and mutualism, even though the organisms differ.

days.guide: Read about California sea otters. Your child explains the otter–urchin–kelp relationship. Check before moving on: ask "What happens to kelp if sea otters disappear?" Look for: Urchins multiply and overgraze kelp, creating 'urchin barrens'.

questions.q: What happens to kelp if sea otters disappear?
questions.a: Urchins multiply and overgraze kelp, creating 'urchin barrens'.

days.guide: Your child writes a prediction of what happens when a predator is removed from an ecosystem. Check before moving on: ask "Possible prediction?" Look for: Prey population rises, overeats its food, then may crash; other species are affected too (trophic cascade).

questions.a: Prey population rises, overeats its food, then may crash; other species are affected too (trophic cascade).

weeks.assessment_key: Survey log: date, time, location, organisms with counts, at least two interactions classified. Prediction rubric: 4 = names predator/prey, predicts prey increase and resource decline with reasoning and a real example (otters/urchins/kelp or wolves/elk in Yellowstone); 2 = prediction without reasoning.

weeks.prep: Yarn, index cards; optional sterilized owl pellet kit (or virtual pellet online), tweezers, gloves; calculator.
misconceptions: Drawing arrows from predator to prey. Arrows show energy flow: from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it.
Thinking all energy moves up a level. Only about 10% is passed on; the rest is used for life processes and lost as heat.

days.guide: Build two chaparral food chains with your child, labeling producers, consumers and decomposers. Check before moving on: ask "Give a chaparral food chain." Look for: Chamise (producer) → brush rabbit (primary consumer) → coyote (secondary consumer); fungi and bacteria decompose them.

questions.a: Chamise (producer) → brush rabbit (primary consumer) → coyote (secondary consumer); fungi and bacteria decompose them.

days.guide: Connect organism cards with yarn into a web. Remove one organism and have your child predict and trace the effects. Check before moving on: ask "If rabbits are removed, what happens?" Look for: Coyotes and hawks lose a food source and decline or switch prey; plants rabbits ate may increase.

questions.q: If rabbits are removed, what happens?
questions.a: Coyotes and hawks lose a food source and decline or switch prey; plants rabbits ate may increase.

days.guide: Your child dissects the pellet, sorts bones, uses a chart to identify prey and builds the owl's food web. Check before moving on: ask "What prey bones are typical?" Look for: Voles, mice and shrews (skulls, jaws, leg bones).

questions.a: Voles, mice and shrews (skulls, jaws, leg bones).

days.guide: Model the 10% rule. Your child calculates energy at each level and draws a pyramid. Check before moving on: ask "Producers have 10,000 kcal. Energy at the third consumer level?" Look for: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kcal.

questions.q: Producers have 10,000 kcal. Energy at the third consumer level?

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Why are there fewer top predators than herbivores?" Look for: Less energy is available at each higher level.

questions.q: Why are there fewer top predators than herbivores?
questions.a: Less energy is available at each higher level.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Arrow direction = energy flow. 2) Producer, consumer, decomposer examples. 3) 10% rule: 5,000 kcal producers → 50 kcal secondary consumers. 4) Pyramid widest at producers. 5) Removing a species affects others.

weeks.prep: Clear jars with lids, soil, bread, apple slices, leaves, spray bottle; magnifier. Do not open moldy jars indoors — mold spores can trigger allergies.
misconceptions: Thinking decomposition destroys matter. Decomposers break it into simpler substances that return to soil and air.
Thinking mold is a plant. Molds are fungi; they don't photosynthesize.

days.guide: Your child sets up jars with bread, apple and leaves — some moist, some dry — labels and predicts which decompose faster. Check before moving on: ask "Which conditions should speed decomposition?" Look for: Moist and warm — decomposers need water and grow faster when warm.

questions.a: Moist and warm — decomposers need water and grow faster when warm.

days.guide: Through a sealed bag, your child views moldy bread with a magnifier and draws thread-like hyphae and spore heads. Check before moving on: ask "What are hyphae?" Look for: The thread-like filaments of a fungus that grow into food and absorb nutrients.

questions.a: The thread-like filaments of a fungus that grow into food and absorb nutrients.

days.guide: Draw the carbon and nitrogen cycles with arrows. Your child labels each step including decomposers. Check before moving on: ask "Role of decomposers in the carbon cycle?" Look for: They break down dead matter and release CO2 through respiration.

questions.q: Role of decomposers in the carbon cycle?
questions.a: They break down dead matter and release CO2 through respiration.
They return nitrogen compounds to the soil for plants to absorb.

days.guide: Your child designs a compost bin and explains how it returns matter to soil. Check before moving on: ask "What does compost need?" Look for: Green (nitrogen-rich) and brown (carbon-rich) materials, moisture, and air.

questions.a: Green (nitrogen-rich) and brown (carbon-rich) materials, moisture, and air.

days.guide: Give the semester checkpoint covering units 1–4. Check before moving on: ask "Why does a balloon of yeast and sugar inflate?" Look for: Yeast respiration produces CO2.

questions.q: Why does a balloon of yeast and sugar inflate?
questions.a: Yeast respiration produces CO2.

weeks.assessment_key: Decomposition observations: dated entries with sketches. Semester checkpoint: particles; elements/compounds; density; chemical vs physical; balancing; conservation of mass; endo/exothermic; photosynthesis/respiration; food webs and 10% rule. Note any topic below 70% for review.

weeks.prep: 2-liter bottle (adult cuts it), gravel, soil, small plants, water, pill bugs or snails from the yard; decomposition jars from week 18.
misconceptions: Calling soil and water 'non-living so unimportant.' Abiotic factors determine what biotic factors can survive.
Thinking a terrarium needs no light because it's sealed. Plants need light to supply energy.

days.guide: Layer gravel, soil, plants and invertebrates; mist and close. Your child diagrams biotic and abiotic parts. Check before moving on: ask "List biotic and abiotic parts." Look for: Biotic: plants, pill bugs, microbes; abiotic: soil minerals, water, air, light, gravel.

questions.a: Biotic: plants, pill bugs, microbes; abiotic: soil minerals, water, air, light, gravel.

days.guide: Your child records changes in each jar and compares moist and dry conditions. Check before moving on: ask "Which decomposed faster and why?" Look for: Moist jars, because decomposers (fungi, bacteria) need water.

questions.a: Moist jars, because decomposers (fungi, bacteria) need water.

days.guide: Your child draws matter-cycling and energy-flow arrows through the terrarium. Check before moving on: ask "Where does energy enter and leave?" Look for: Enters as light; leaves as heat.

questions.q: Where does energy enter and leave?
questions.a: Enters as light; leaves as heat.

days.guide: Review vocabulary and practice data-analysis questions together. Check before moving on: ask "Define 'decomposer'." Look for: Organism that breaks down dead matter (fungi, bacteria).

questions.a: Organism that breaks down dead matter (fungi, bacteria).

days.guide: Give the unit 4 test; continue weekly terrarium observations. Check before moving on: ask "What is a trophic cascade?" Look for: A chain of effects through a food web when one population changes.

questions.a: A chain of effects through a food web when one population changes.

weeks.assessment_key: Terrarium diagram: labeled biotic/abiotic, matter arrows cycling, energy in as light and out as heat. Unit 4 test: interaction types, limiting factors, food web arrows, 10% rule, decomposers' role.

weeks.prep: Rock samples from yard or a store rock kit, steel nail, copper penny, unglazed tile (back of a bathroom tile), glass plate (adult), vinegar, dropper; salt or sugar, jar, string, pencil.
misconceptions: Thinking minerals and rocks are the same. A mineral is a naturally formed, inorganic solid with a definite composition and crystal structure; rocks are made of one or more minerals.
Thinking streak color always equals the sample's color. Pyrite looks gold but leaves a greenish-black streak.

days.guide: Demonstrate luster, streak and the scratch test. Your child tests each sample: fingernail (~2.5), penny (~3.5), nail (~5.5), records hardness range. Check before moving on: ask "A mineral is scratched by a nail but not by a penny. Hardness?" Look for: Between about 3.5 and 5.5.

questions.q: A mineral is scratched by a nail but not by a penny. Hardness?
questions.a: Between about 3.5 and 5.5.
The color of a mineral's powder when rubbed on unglazed tile.

days.guide: Dissolve salt (or sugar) in hot water until no more dissolves (adult heats), hang a string, and let it sit. Your child records crystal growth daily. Check before moving on: ask "How does this model mineral formation?" Look for: As water evaporates or cools, dissolved minerals come out of solution and form crystals.

questions.q: How does this model mineral formation?
questions.a: As water evaporates or cools, dissolved minerals come out of solution and form crystals.

days.guide: Teach the three rock types. Your child classifies samples with an ID key. Check before moving on: ask "Granite?" Look for: Igneous (intrusive, cooled slowly underground — big crystals).

questions.a: Igneous (intrusive, cooled slowly underground — big crystals).
Sedimentary.

days.guide: Drop vinegar on each rock. Your child identifies fizzers and explains. Check before moving on: ask "What does fizzing show?" Look for: Calcium carbonate (calcite/limestone) reacting with acid to make CO2 gas.

questions.a: Calcium carbonate (calcite/limestone) reacting with acid to make CO2 gas.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Marble — rock type?" Look for: Metamorphic (from limestone).

questions.a: Metamorphic (from limestone).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Mineral definition. 2) Mohs hardness: talc 1, diamond 10. 3) Streak test. 4) Igneous = cooled magma/lava; sedimentary = compacted sediments; metamorphic = changed by heat and pressure. 5) Limestone fizzes. ID chart: each sample with luster, streak, hardness, type.

weeks.prep: Crayons (3 colors), pencil sharpener or grater, aluminum foil, hot water (adult); sugar cubes, jar with lid, timer; rock cycle diagram.
misconceptions: Thinking the rock cycle is a fixed circle. Any rock type can become any other by different processes.
Forgetting energy sources. The sun drives weathering/erosion; Earth's internal heat drives melting and metamorphism.

days.guide: Your child shaves crayons (weathering), presses layers in foil (compaction → sedimentary), presses with warm hands/hot water (metamorphic), adult melts in foil boat in hot water (igneous after cooling). Check before moving on: ask "What did pressing represent?" Look for: Compaction and cementation forming sedimentary rock.

questions.a: Compaction and cementation forming sedimentary rock.
Igneous rock forming from magma.

days.guide: Your child labels a rock-cycle diagram with energy source for each process. Check before moving on: ask "Energy source for erosion?" Look for: The sun (drives water cycle and wind) and gravity.

questions.a: The sun (drives water cycle and wind) and gravity.
Earth's internal heat.

days.guide: Shake sugar cubes for 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes. Your child weighs remaining cube mass or counts fragments and graphs. Check before moving on: ask "Result?" Look for: Longer shaking breaks more pieces off — more mechanical weathering.

questions.a: Longer shaking breaks more pieces off — more mechanical weathering.

days.guide: Research serpentine and Sierra granite. Your child places each in the cycle. Check before moving on: ask "Serpentine rock type?" Look for: Metamorphic — formed from ocean-floor rock altered by water and pressure.

questions.a: Metamorphic — formed from ocean-floor rock altered by water and pressure.
Igneous — magma cooled slowly underground, later uplifted and exposed by erosion.

days.guide: Your child draws a full rock cycle with 8+ processes. Check before moving on: ask "Name 8 processes." Look for: Weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation, metamorphism, melting, cooling/crystallization, uplift.

questions.a: Weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation, metamorphism, melting, cooling/crystallization, uplift.

weeks.assessment_key: Rock-cycle model rubric: 4 = all three rock types, 8+ correctly labeled processes, arrows showing multiple paths, energy sources noted; 3 = 6–7 processes; 2 = only circular path; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Baking pan or plastic bin, sand, soil, watering can, books to prop slope; ice cubes with sand frozen in, clay or play dough; photos of Yosemite Valley.
misconceptions: Thinking erosion and weathering are the same. Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves the pieces.
Thinking all landforms take millions of years. Some (landslides, floods) happen in seconds to days.

days.guide: Prop the pan at low slope; pour water steadily from the top. Your child sketches channels and the delta. Check before moving on: ask "Where is sediment deposited?" Look for: Where water slows — at the bottom/outlet, forming a delta.

questions.a: Where water slows — at the bottom/outlet, forming a delta.

days.guide: Repeat with steeper slope. Your child compares. Check before moving on: ask "Effect of steeper slope?" Look for: Faster water, deeper channels, more erosion and larger deposits.

questions.a: Faster water, deeper channels, more erosion and larger deposits.

days.guide: Drag the sandy ice cube over clay. Your child compares the scratches to Yosemite Valley's U-shape. Check before moving on: ask "How did glaciers shape Yosemite Valley?" Look for: Glaciers carved a V-shaped river valley into a wide U-shape and polished granite.

questions.q: How did glaciers shape Yosemite Valley?
questions.a: Glaciers carved a V-shaped river valley into a wide U-shape and polished granite.

days.guide: Your child places events on a timeline from seconds to millions of years. Check before moving on: ask "Fast and slow examples?" Look for: Landslide (seconds–minutes), flood (days), canyon formation (millions of years).

questions.a: Landslide (seconds–minutes), flood (days), canyon formation (millions of years).

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on a California landform shaped by water. Check before moving on: ask "Example claim?" Look for: The Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta formed from river sediment deposited where rivers slowed.

questions.a: The Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta formed from river sediment deposited where rivers slowed.

weeks.assessment_key: Stream-table data: sketches/measurements comparing slopes. CER rubric: 4 = accurate claim, at least two pieces of specific evidence from the investigation (numbers/observations), reasoning that links evidence to the scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect.

weeks.prep: Clear cup, gravel, sand, clay, water, food coloring, sponge; short readings on California gold and Central Valley oil; USGS mineral resource map.
misconceptions: Thinking groundwater is an underground lake. It fills spaces between sediment grains and cracks in rock.
Thinking resources are spread evenly. They form only where specific geologic processes happened.

days.guide: Read about California gold. Your child explains how gold formed and concentrated. Check before moving on: ask "How did gold form?" Look for: Hot fluids from magma deposited gold in quartz veins in the Sierra foothills.

questions.a: Hot fluids from magma deposited gold in quartz veins in the Sierra foothills.
Weathering freed gold; since it's very dense, it settled in stream gravels (placer deposits).

days.guide: Layer gravel, sand, clay in a cup; add water and colored 'pollution'. Your child observes spreading. Check before moving on: ask "Why does pollution spread?" Look for: Water moves through connected pores in sand and gravel, carrying pollution.

questions.a: Water moves through connected pores in sand and gravel, carrying pollution.

days.guide: Read about oil in the Central Valley. Your child maps fossil fuel locations. Check before moving on: ask "How did oil form?" Look for: Tiny marine organisms buried in sediment were heated and pressurized over millions of years.

questions.a: Tiny marine organisms buried in sediment were heated and pressurized over millions of years.

days.guide: Your child analyzes the USGS map. Check before moving on: ask "Why are resources unevenly distributed?" Look for: They form only where specific past geologic conditions occurred.

questions.a: They form only where specific past geologic conditions occurred.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "What is an aquifer?" Look for: Underground layer of permeable rock/sediment holding groundwater.

questions.a: Underground layer of permeable rock/sediment holding groundwater.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Aquifer definition. 2) Gold in quartz veins, concentrated as placer. 3) Oil from buried marine organisms. 4) Uneven distribution due to geology. 5) Clay is less permeable.

weeks.prep: Chocolate chip cookies (two types), toothpicks, graph paper; Central Valley subsidence data (USGS).
misconceptions: Thinking extracting resources is free once found.
Thinking subsidence reverses when pumping stops. Compacted clay often doesn't rebound.

days.guide: Your child 'buys' land (cookie), mines chips with toothpicks, tracks costs and profits. Check before moving on: ask "What does the crumbled cookie represent?" Look for: Environmental damage/land disturbance from mining.

questions.q: What does the crumbled cookie represent?
questions.a: Environmental damage/land disturbance from mining.

days.guide: Your child graphs subsidence data. Check before moving on: ask "Why does land sink?" Look for: Pumping groundwater removes water from clay layers, which compact.

questions.a: Pumping groundwater removes water from clay layers, which compact.

days.guide: Your child writes why one California resource is found where it is. Check before moving on: ask "Example?" Look for: Gold in the Sierra foothills from quartz veins.

questions.a: Gold in the Sierra foothills from quartz veins.

days.guide: Review practice set. Check before moving on: ask "Igneous vs sedimentary formation?" Look for: Cooling magma vs compacted sediments.

questions.a: Cooling magma vs compacted sediments.

days.guide: Give unit 5 test. Check before moving on: ask "What fizzes with vinegar?" Look for: Limestone/calcite.

questions.a: Limestone/calcite.

weeks.assessment_key: Cookie analysis: profit calculation and environmental cost discussion. Unit 5 test: minerals, rock cycle, weathering/erosion/deposition, resources, aquifers.

weeks.prep: Colored play dough, plastic knife, clear jar with lid, sand, soil, gravel, water; Grand Canyon cross-section diagram (NPS); two cliff diagrams with index fossils.
misconceptions: Thinking the top layer is oldest. By superposition, in undisturbed layers the bottom is oldest.
Thinking a fault or intrusion is older than the layers it cuts. Cross-cutting features are younger.

days.guide: Shake sand, soil and gravel in water and let settle. Your child sketches the layers. Check before moving on: ask "Which settles first?" Look for: Gravel (largest, heaviest), then sand, then fine soil/clay on top.

questions.a: Gravel (largest, heaviest), then sand, then fine soil/clay on top.

days.guide: Build 4 play-dough layers, cut a fault, push in an 'intrusion'. A family member sequences events; your child checks. Check before moving on: ask "Order of events?" Look for: Layers deposited bottom to top, then fault and intrusion (whichever cuts the other is younger).

questions.a: Layers deposited bottom to top, then fault and intrusion (whichever cuts the other is younger).

days.guide: Your child orders Grand Canyon layers and events. Check before moving on: ask "Oldest rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon?" Look for: Vishnu Schist (metamorphic, about 1.7 billion years old).

questions.q: Oldest rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon?
questions.a: Vishnu Schist (metamorphic, about 1.7 billion years old).
Kaibab Limestone.

days.guide: Model correlating layers using an index fossil. Your child matches layers between two cliffs. Check before moving on: ask "What makes a good index fossil?" Look for: Widespread, lived a short time, easy to recognize.

questions.q: What makes a good index fossil?
questions.a: Widespread, lived a short time, easy to recognize.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Law of superposition?" Look for: In undisturbed layers, the oldest is at the bottom.

questions.a: In undisturbed layers, the oldest is at the bottom.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Superposition. 2) Original horizontality (layers deposited flat). 3) Cross-cutting relationships (feature cutting layers is younger). 4) Index fossils correlate layers. 5) Sequence a diagram correctly.

weeks.prep: Roll of receipt paper or toilet paper, meter stick, markers; 100 pennies, cup, graph paper.
misconceptions: Thinking humans and dinosaurs lived together. Non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago; humans appeared about 300,000 years ago.
Thinking half-life means all is gone after two half-lives. Half of what remains decays each half-life.

days.guide: Lay out 46 m (1 m = 100 million years). Your child marks Earth's formation (4.6 bya), first life (~3.5–3.8 bya), Cambrian explosion (~539 mya), dinosaurs (~230–66 mya), humans. Check before moving on: ask "How far from the end is the dinosaur extinction?" Look for: 66 million years = 0.66 m.

questions.q: How far from the end is the dinosaur extinction?
questions.a: 66 million years = 0.66 m.
About 3 mm from the end (300,000 years).

days.guide: Your child calculates humans' fraction of Earth's history and writes a reflection. Check before moving on: ask "Fraction?" Look for: 300,000 / 4,600,000,000 ≈ 0.0065% of Earth's history.
Flip 100 pennies; remove tails each round. Your child records and graphs. Check before moving on: ask "About how many remain after 3 rounds?" Look for: About 12–13 (100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5).

questions.q: About how many remain after 3 rounds?

questions.a: Measure the ratio of parent to daughter atoms; knowing the half-life gives the age.

days.guide: Read about the five mass extinctions. Your child labels them. Check before moving on: ask "Largest?" Look for: End-Permian (~252 mya), 'the Great Dying'.

questions.a: End-Permian (~252 mya), 'the Great Dying'.
End-Cretaceous (~66 mya), asteroid impact, killed non-avian dinosaurs.

days.guide: Your child explains how strata and fossils built the time scale. Check before moving on: ask "Key idea?" Look for: Relative dating ordered layers and fossil changes; radiometric dating added absolute ages.

questions.a: Relative dating ordered layers and fossil changes; radiometric dating added absolute ages.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: scale correct (1 m = 100 million years), events placed accurately, five extinctions labeled (end-Ordovician ~445, Late Devonian ~372, end-Permian ~252, end-Triassic ~201, end-Cretaceous ~66 mya). Explanation rubric: superposition, index fossils, radiometric dating.

weeks.prep: Plaster of Paris or salt dough, shells, leaves, petroleum jelly, paper cups; Smithsonian Learning Lab fossil images; La Brea Tar Pits website.
misconceptions: Thinking fossils are always actual bones. Most are mineral replacements, molds, casts or traces.
Thinking the fossil record is complete. Fossilization is rare.

days.guide: Coat a shell with petroleum jelly, press into dough (mold), fill with plaster (cast). Your child labels each. Check before moving on: ask "Mold vs cast?" Look for: Mold is the hollow impression; cast is the filled replica.

questions.a: Mold is the hollow impression; cast is the filled replica.

days.guide: Compare body, trace, mold, cast and amber fossils. Check before moving on: ask "Footprint?" Look for: Trace fossil.

questions.a: Trace fossil.
Preserved remains in hardened tree resin.

days.guide: Explore La Brea Tar Pits. Your child explains what it reveals about Ice Age LA. Check before moving on: ask "Animals found?" Look for: Saber-toothed cats, dire wolves (most common), mammoths, giant ground sloths.

questions.a: Saber-toothed cats, dire wolves (most common), mammoths, giant ground sloths.
Predators came to eat trapped animals and got stuck too.

days.guide: Your child analyzes a chart of appearances and extinctions. Check before moving on: ask "Pattern?" Look for: Life diversified over time with sudden losses at mass extinctions, followed by new diversification.

questions.a: Life diversified over time with sudden losses at mass extinctions, followed by new diversification.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Where do fossils usually form?" Look for: Sedimentary rock.

questions.a: Sedimentary rock.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: fossil types, why sedimentary, La Brea evidence, diversification/extinction pattern, fossil record incomplete. Models labeled mold and cast.

weeks.prep: Printed continent outlines with fossil and rock evidence; scissors; paper strips, shoebox; seafloor age map and ocean depth map (NOAA).
misconceptions: Thinking continents float on the ocean. Plates are slabs of lithosphere moving over the asthenosphere.
Thinking Wegener's idea was accepted immediately.

days.guide: Your child cuts and fits continents using fossil and rock clues. Check before moving on: ask "Mesosaurus fossils in South America and Africa show?" Look for: The continents were once joined.

questions.q: Mesosaurus fossils in South America and Africa show?
questions.a: The continents were once joined.

days.guide: Read about Wegener. Your child lists four evidence lines and why rejected. Check before moving on: ask "Four lines?" Look for: Continent fit, matching fossils, matching rock formations/mountains, past climate evidence (glacial deposits in tropics, coal in Antarctica).

questions.a: Continent fit, matching fossils, matching rock formations/mountains, past climate evidence (glacial deposits in tropics, coal in Antarctica).
He could not explain the mechanism for movement.

days.guide: Pull paper strips up through a slit to model spreading; color magnetic stripes. Check before moving on: ask "What do symmetric stripes show?" Look for: New seafloor forms at ridges and spreads both ways, recording magnetic reversals.

questions.a: New seafloor forms at ridges and spreads both ways, recording magnetic reversals.

days.guide: Your child analyzes seafloor age and depth maps. Check before moving on: ask "Where is youngest seafloor?" Look for: At mid-ocean ridges.

questions.a: At mid-ocean ridges.
Near trenches/continents.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on whether continents have moved. Check before moving on: ask "What would a strong claim and evidence look like?" Look for: Claim: the continents have moved over millions of years. Evidence: Mesosaurus/Glossopteris fossils match across oceans; seafloor is youngest at ridges and older away from them; magnetic stripes are symmetric on both sides of ridges.

questions.q: What would a strong claim and evidence look like?
questions.a: Claim: the continents have moved over millions of years. Evidence: Mesosaurus/Glossopteris fossils match across oceans; seafloor is youngest at ridges and older away from them; magnetic stripes are symmetric on both sides of ridges.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = accurate claim, at least two pieces of specific evidence from the investigation (numbers/observations), reasoning that links evidence to the scientific principle; 3 = claim and evidence, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or incorrect. Proficient uses three types: fossil/rock matches, seafloor age pattern, magnetic striping.

weeks.prep: Graham crackers, frosting, wax paper; USGS 'Latest Earthquakes' map; world map; calculator.
misconceptions: Thinking California will 'fall into the ocean.' The Pacific Plate slides northwest past North America.
Thinking earthquakes are random.

days.guide: Spread frosting on wax paper (the asthenosphere) and lay two graham-cracker halves on it. Your child models convergent (push together — crackers buckle or one slides under), divergent (pull apart — frosting shows the gap) and transform (slide past — edges catch and jerk) boundaries and sketches each. Check before moving on: ask "San Andreas boundary type?" Look for: Transform.

questions.a: Transform.

days.guide: Open the USGS Latest Earthquakes map (past 30 days, magnitude 2.5+). Your child plots or marks 20–30 quakes on a world map and traces the lines where they cluster, then compares with a plate boundary map. Check before moving on: ask "Pattern?" Look for: Earthquakes cluster along plate boundaries (Ring of Fire).

questions.a: Earthquakes cluster along plate boundaries (Ring of Fire).

days.guide: Explain that the Pacific Plate (with LA) slides northwest relative to the North American Plate along the San Andreas. Your child calculates movement at 5 cm/yr over 1,000 years and converts to meters. Check before moving on: ask "5 cm/yr × 1,000 years?" Look for: 5,000 cm = 50 m.

Show maps of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades. Your child explains how subduction produced the magma for Sierra granite and Mount Shasta, and how later faulting uplifted the Sierra. Check before moving on: ask "Sierra Nevada?" Look for: Granite from subduction magma, later uplifted and tilted by faulting.

questions.a: Granite from subduction magma, later uplifted and tilted by faulting.
Volcano from Juan de Fuca Plate subducting under North America (Cascade arc).

days.guide: Give the quiz on boundary types and California geology without notes. Review the earthquake map together. Check before moving on: ask "Divergent example?" Look for: Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

questions.a: Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: three boundary types with examples, San Andreas transform, 50 m in 1,000 yrs, Shasta from subduction, earthquakes at boundaries. Map: plotted quakes with boundaries identified.

weeks.prep: Poster paper; toothpicks, mini marshmallows, gelatin pan (shake table); landform research materials.
misconceptions: Thinking big changes need big events.
Thinking tall buildings are always less safe.

days.guide: Brainstorm Earth processes together. Your child makes a chart placing each on axes of time (seconds to millions of years) and size (local to continental). Check before moving on: ask "Example?" Look for: Landslide (minutes), river canyon (millions of years), mountain building (tens of millions).

questions.a: Landslide (minutes), river canyon (millions of years), mountain building (tens of millions).

days.guide: Make gelatin in a pan the night before. Your child builds a toothpick-and-marshmallow structure, tests it by shaking the pan, then improves it with triangles or a wider base and retests. Check before moving on: ask "Design features that help?" Look for: Triangles (bracing), wide base, low center of mass.

questions.a: Triangles (bracing), wide base, low center of mass.

days.guide: Your child picks a California landform and writes its geologic history in order, naming processes at different time scales. Check that each step names a process (deposition, uplift, erosion, glaciation). Check before moving on: ask "Yosemite example?" Look for: Granite formed underground, uplifted, eroded by rivers, carved by glaciers.

questions.a: Granite formed underground, uplifted, eroded by rivers, carved by glaciers.

days.guide: Your child works a unit 6 practice set; review answers together and re-teach any missed topic. Check before moving on: ask "What is a transform boundary?" Look for: Plates slide past.

questions.a: Plates slide past.

days.guide: Give the unit 6 test independently. Check before moving on: ask "Oldest layer?" Look for: Bottom.

questions.a: Bottom.

weeks.assessment_key: Landform history rubric: sequence at multiple time scales. Unit 6 test: relative dating, time scale, fossils, plate tectonics, California geology.

weeks.prep: Before/after images of a California wildfire area (e.g., NASA Earth Observatory); succession reading; data on quagga mussels or Argentine ants (CA Dept. of Fish and Wildlife or UC IPM); graph paper.
misconceptions: Thinking fire only destroys. Many California ecosystems (chaparral, some pines) are adapted to fire and recover through succession.
Confusing correlation with cause. Data must link the change to the population effect.

days.guide: Compare images. Your child predicts which populations decline and which increase after fire. Check before moving on: ask "Which might increase soon after fire?" Look for: Grasses and fire-following wildflowers, and animals that eat them; also woodpeckers feeding on insects in dead trees.

questions.q: Which might increase soon after fire?
questions.a: Grasses and fire-following wildflowers, and animals that eat them; also woodpeckers feeding on insects in dead trees.

days.guide: Read about succession. Your child sequences stages. Check before moving on: ask "Typical sequence after fire?" Look for: Bare/ash → grasses and wildflowers → shrubs → young trees → mature forest or chaparral.

questions.a: Bare/ash → grasses and wildflowers → shrubs → young trees → mature forest or chaparral.

days.guide: Your child graphs data on an invasive species and native species decline. Check before moving on: ask "How do Argentine ants affect coast horned lizards?" Look for: They displace native ants the lizards eat, so lizards decline.

questions.q: How do Argentine ants affect coast horned lizards?
questions.a: They displace native ants the lizards eat, so lizards decline.
Filter out plankton, clog water pipes, outcompete native species.

days.guide: Your child writes a data-based argument on how one change affected a population. Check before moving on: ask "What makes it data-based?" Look for: Specific numbers or graph trends cited as evidence.

questions.a: Specific numbers or graph trends cited as evidence.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "What is an invasive species?" Look for: A non-native species that spreads and harms the ecosystem.

questions.a: A non-native species that spreads and harms the ecosystem.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: succession stages, fire-adapted ecosystems, invasive species definition and example, predicting population changes from disruptions. Argument rubric: claim, data cited, reasoning about cause.

weeks.prep: Hula hoop or string square (1 m²), field guide or iNaturalist app, clipboard; reading on pollinator decline.
misconceptions: Thinking biodiversity means only number of species. It includes how evenly individuals are spread among species.
Thinking ecosystem services are free and unlimited.

days.guide: Your child lists services with California examples. Check before moving on: ask "Pollination example?" Look for: Bees pollinate Central Valley almonds.

questions.a: Bees pollinate Central Valley almonds.
Wetlands filter runoff before it reaches the Bay.

days.guide: Survey two 1-m² plots (lawn vs garden/wild). Your child counts species and individuals. Check before moving on: ask "Why compare two locations?" Look for: To see how habitat affects biodiversity.

questions.a: To see how habitat affects biodiversity.

days.guide: Your child calculates species ÷ individuals for each plot. Check before moving on: ask "8 species, 40 individuals?" Look for: 0.2.

questions.a: The one with the higher index.

days.guide: Read about pollinators. Your child explains food crop effects. Check before moving on: ask "Why worry about bee decline?" Look for: About one-third of our food crops depend on animal pollinators.

questions.a: About one-third of our food crops depend on animal pollinators.

days.guide: Your child writes a report comparing plots. Check before moving on: ask "Report sections?" Look for: Question, method, data, comparison, conclusion.

questions.a: Question, method, data, comparison, conclusion.

weeks.assessment_key: Report rubric: data tables, index calculation, comparison, explanation of habitat differences.

weeks.prep: World population data (1800–today); online ecological footprint calculator; household water and electric bills.
misconceptions: Thinking population has always grown fast. Growth was slow until the 1800s, then accelerated.
Thinking one person's use doesn't matter. Multiply by millions.

days.guide: Your child graphs world population. Check before moving on: ask "Approximate values?" Look for: ~1 billion (1800), 2 billion (1927), 6 billion (1999), 8 billion (2022).

questions.a: ~1 billion (1800), 2 billion (1927), 6 billion (1999), 8 billion (2022).
Slow then steep (exponential-like), recently slowing.

days.guide: Use a footprint calculator. Your child compares with world averages. Check before moving on: ask "What does a footprint measure?" Look for: Land/resources needed to support one person's lifestyle.

questions.a: Land/resources needed to support one person's lifestyle.

days.guide: Your child calculates per-person water and electricity use from bills. Check before moving on: ask "300 kWh per month for 4 people?" Look for: 75 kWh per person per month.

questions.a: 75 kWh per person per month.

days.guide: Your child writes an argument on consumption affecting one Earth system. Check before moving on: ask "Example?" Look for: Increased energy use burns fossil fuels, adding CO2 to the atmosphere.

questions.a: Increased energy use burns fossil fuels, adding CO2 to the atmosphere.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Why does population matter?" Look for: More people means more resource use.

questions.a: More people means more resource use.

weeks.assessment_key: Household audit: per-person calculations correct. Argument rubric: claim, evidence, reasoning on Earth system impact. Quiz: population trend, footprint, consumption impacts.
